points.heading: Week overview
points.body:
This week we learned to tell time in Spanish. A verb form shows when an action happens. Simple forms have one word, such as «canté». Compound forms join haber to a participle, such as «he cantado». The form changes what part of the story stands out.

Compare «Terminé ayer» and «He terminado». The first closes an action yesterday; the second says that the result matters now.

Practice: Explain the difference between «canté» and «he cantado» to someone at home using an example from your week.

Common mistake: Repeating tense names without making a sentence that shows their meaning.

points.heading: Overview: one word
points.body:
Simple tenses use one verb word. With cantar, the five forms are canto, cantaba, canté, cantaré, and cantaría. They show now, an ongoing past, a finished past, the future, or a possibility.

«Cantaba» describes a habit or background, while «canté» tells a finished event. Ask whether the action stayed open or ended.

Practice: Say the five “I” forms and write one short sentence that shows when each action happens.

Common mistake: Using «cantaba» for a closed event yesterday.

points.heading: Overview: two words
points.body:
Compound tenses use two pieces. Haber is the helper word, and a participle is the completed verb form, such as cantado, comido, or vivido. In «he cantado», the helper changes for the person, but cantado stays the same.

«Había cantado» places the action before another past moment, while «habría cantado» describes what would happen in a condition.

Practice: Write three sentences with «he cantado», «había cantado», and «habría cantado» as parts of one story.

Common mistake: Changing the participle for the person. Keep «cantado» unchanged.

points.heading: Overview: choosing
points.body:
Choosing a tense means deciding what you want to show. Ask whether the action is closed, whether its result matters now, or whether it is a background or habit. These questions guide your choice.

Words such as ayer, ya, and cuando are useful clues, but read the whole sentence before deciding.

Practice: Sort five of your own sentences into closed action, present result, and background or habit. Explain one choice aloud.

Common mistake: Choosing a form without noticing time clues such as ayer, ya, or cuando.

points.heading: Synthesis
points.body:
The main idea is to tell a clear story. First decide whether you need a simple or compound form, then choose the time that fits. Grammar names can help, but a clear example proves that you understand.

Read this pair: «Ayer jugué en el parque. Hoy he contado el partido». Jugué closes yesterday’s action; he contado connects a completed action to now.

Practice: Write a four-sentence paragraph about your week. Use at least one simple form and one compound form, then underline the time clues.

Common mistake: Memorizing a list without using the forms in your own sentences.

lesson.summary: This review joins simple and compound indicative tenses. Choose them by deciding whether you are telling a finished action, a result that matters now, or a past background.
